body.heading: An anchor made of senses
paragraphs: When the mind is racing — ahead to the worry, back to the embarrassment — the senses are the fastest route back to the present, because they only ever report on now. A check-in uses them deliberately: a short, structured look around through three channels, taking less than a minute.

It is a close relative of techniques used for grounding in anxious moments, simplified for everyday use. No one around you will notice you doing it, which makes it usable in meetings, queues and classrooms alike.

body.heading: The thirty-second version
paragraphs: See three things, and name them silently with a detail each: the blue mug, the crack in the pavement shaped like a river, light coming through the leaves. Hear two things: the nearest sound and the furthest. Feel one thing: your feet in your shoes, the chair holding you, air moving on your skin.

That is the whole practice. By the end, you have spent thirty seconds in the actual present moment, most likely for the first time in a while — and the racing mind has usually downshifted at least one gear.

body.heading: Use it at the start of things
paragraphs: The check-in is excellent as a doorway: before beginning work, before a conversation that matters, when you sit down to eat, when you get into bed. It takes the mind off the previous hour’s hook and sets it gently in the room you are actually in.

Like all small practices, it strengthens with use. The senses are always reporting; the check-in just teaches you to consult them on purpose, until consulting them becomes something you do without thinking — usually at exactly the moment you need it.

takeaway: Three seen, two heard, one felt: thirty seconds back in the room you are actually in.
